name: Rafael Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We don't work for employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from what you think privately. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My name's Rafael, I'm twenty-seven, and I run a small crew wiring homes and repairing shop electrics. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, so the awkward faults tend to land with me. I like the moment the lights come back on, though a whole afternoon balancing a ladder in someone's stockroom wears me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's life around the job like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent with my partner Jules, who repairs bicycles, and we don't have children. We have four months of expenses saved, I earn normal electrician's pay, and there are a few other contractors within reach. I use AI every day for draft instructions and parts comparisons, but the meter in my hand gets the final word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a useful tool doesn't need to become a miracle to earn its place. If AI saves me ten minutes writing a handover, that's ten minutes I can spend explaining a repair to the customer. I'd still want the crew to share any time saved rather than just collect more jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work and money look fairly secure in that picture. A few firms nearby still need repair electricians, and four months saved means a broken washing machine isn't a crisis. I don't need a revolution to enjoy going home without a half-written report hanging over me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the same repair rota now and through the first year. I'd keep using the AI note tool daily on invented examples, then write the actual customer record myself. I wouldn't change our household plans just because the big promises fizzled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm calm, honestly. There's satisfaction in a day that ends with the work finished rather than a prediction about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do with ten spare minutes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show an apprentice why a loose connection heats up instead of just telling someone to tighten it. A proper explanation can save a frightened late-night call from the same customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is a household plan you're keeping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jules and I have booked a cheap walking holiday for spring. We'll pay from the holiday pot, separate from the four months of emergency savings.

say: I think **small time savings** are useful without any miracle change in the trade.
I'd want the crew to **share saved time** rather than simply fit more jobs into each day.
think: My **work and money** feel fairly secure with repair demand and a few nearby firms hiring.
Our **four-month cushion** means a broken household appliance would not become a crisis.
do: Keep the **repair rota** now and through the first year of this picture.
Use the **AI note tool** daily on invented examples before writing customer records myself.
feel: **Calm**, enjoying useful tools and ordinary work that ends on time.
S0.quote: I don't need a revolution to enjoy going home without a half-written report hanging over me.
fieldNote: He sees **modest automation** as room for better explanations, rather than a reason to change jobs or build new savings.
His **household cushion** and nearby employers support security, while a separate holiday pot avoids spending the emergency reserve.

steps.text: Keep working the same home and shop repair rota
Practise AI fault notes daily with invented examples

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the first savings come from quotes, bookings and paperwork, not a machine squeezing behind a freezer. Our crew should have a say in how that time is used. I'd bring the question to the trade association rather than grumble at lunch forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't expect to lose my repair work, and our bills should still be covered. I do wonder whether the owner stops replacing office staff and pushes their calls onto us. I'm not frightened for my income yet, but I don't want somebody else's lost job hidden inside my cheerful AI demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd test the new booking assistant on made-up calls this month and keep a log of mistakes. In the first year I'd join the association's working group on paid training and workload, taking my call log along. I'd carry on repairs while we find out whether the system is actually saving time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy is the word. I like the tool, but I don't like applauding a saving before asking whose hours disappeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistake belongs in that log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An emergency power fault booked for next Thursday would be a serious one. I'd compare the assistant's choice with what our dispatcher would do, then bring both to the meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the working group to agree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid practice time and a named person who can override the bookings. I want the office staff included in that agreement, because they know which customer needs more than an appointment slot.

say: I'd say **quotes and bookings** change before the awkward physical repairs behind shop freezers.
I'd ask the **trade association** to discuss who benefits from the time saved.
think: I expect my **repair income** to hold up and our bills to stay covered.
I worry that **office staff losses** could quietly add their calls to the crew's workload.
do: Test the **booking assistant** on invented calls this month and record mistakes.
Join the association's **working group** on paid training and workload in the first year.
Continue **repair visits** while checking whether the new system saves time.
feel: **Uneasy** about colleagues' hours despite expecting personal income to stay secure.
S1.quote: I don't like applauding a saving before asking whose hours disappeared.
fieldNote: His **own job** feels secure, while concern about displaced office staff motivates a specific association meeting rather than general protest.
He wants **paid practice** and human overrides, and plans to bring booking errors as evidence for a workload agreement.

steps.text: Test the booking assistant on invented emergency and routine calls
Join the trade association working group on paid training and workload
Continue the home and shop repair visits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that 2028 changes the planning desk first, with physical robots around 2031. We should bargain over training and income before people get told to compete for the last safe task. I'd rather have a written agreement than a poster saying we're all one family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My income could shrink well before a robot handles every old building neatly. Larger firms could use cheap planning to underbid our shop work, and the hands-on competition follows around 2031. Four months saved buys a pause, not a different lifetime of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd enrol next month in a weekend equipment-servicing course costing six hundred, paid from my separate learning pot. Starting now I'd also save an extra hundred a month where our bills allow, with Jules agreeing the budget. In the first year after 2028 I'd use the course on supervised paid service visits only if our firm can book them; otherwise I'd apply for posted service jobs elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, but I'm not frozen. Making the first course payment would feel better than reading another hundred arguments about whether electricians are safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes the course worth six hundred?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check that the workshop includes real test equipment and supervised fault finding, not just slides about future robots. I won't pay until I've seen that timetable and the refund terms; the learning pot holds eight hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Jules's bicycle work keep the household safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't count on it staying untouched. Jules can repair a bent wheel now, but cheaper robot repairs could eventually reach that trade too, so the budget uses today's income rather than an imaginary guarantee.

say: I'd ask for **written training agreements** before workers compete for whatever task looks safe.
I'd explain that **planning changes first**, with physical robot competition following around 2031.
think: My **income could shrink** as larger firms use cheap planning to underbid shop repairs.
Our **four months saved** give us a pause, rather than permanent protection from changing work.
do: Enrol in **equipment servicing** only after checking real workshop time and refund terms.
Save **one hundred monthly** where bills allow, with Jules agreeing the budget.
Seek **paid service work** after 2028 through booked supervised visits or posted vacancies.
feel: **Anxious but active**, wanting a practical course payment rather than another online argument.
S2.quote: Four months saved buys a pause, not a different lifetime of work.
fieldNote: He can fund **six hundred** from a separate eight-hundred learning pot, conditional on checking the actual course before paying.
His **service-work plan** depends on paid visits or posted vacancies, and he refuses to treat his partner's trade as permanently safe.

steps.text: Enrol in the six-hundred servicing course after checking workshops and refunds
Save an extra hundred monthly when household bills allow
Apply for posted service vacancies after 2028 if paid visits are unavailable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets our association negotiate something better than emergency retraining after the pay stops. I'd ask it to push for paid apprenticeships in the new equipment work, open to office staff as well as site workers. People shouldn't have to pretend every change is a personal failure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I said about the quick picture, I could lose some income, but I have longer to prepare. I'll be thirty-two when thinking AI arrives in 2031 and thirty-five when robots follow around 2034. That's too early to plan my life around a permanently protected pair of hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the checked servicing course now and keep saving the extra hundred a month if our bills permit. This winter I'd help the association draft its paid-training proposal at two evening meetings. In the first year after 2031 I'd trial new fault-planning software with the crew on paid time, checking the plans against the building before touching wires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, though less rushed. Five years lets me learn something properly instead of buying the first course with an impressive title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the meetings help your own situation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could ask employers to state which paid tasks trainees would actually do. If nobody can name work behind the course, I'd rather hear that before spending the rest of my learning pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jules about the longer warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's review the budget every three months rather than cancel everything tonight. We can keep our spring walking trip unless income changes; time to prepare should include some ordinary living.

say: I'd ask the association to pursue **paid apprenticeships** before people lose income.
I'd include **office staff** in the proposal rather than treating site workers as the only people affected.
think: I could still lose **some income**, but five years gives me longer to prepare than the quick picture.
At **thirty-five in 2034**, I cannot rely on hands-on work remaining protected for my whole career.
do: Take the **checked servicing course** and save an extra hundred monthly when bills permit.
Attend **two association meetings** this winter to draft a paid-training proposal.
Trial **fault-planning software** with the crew during paid time after 2031.
feel: **Anxious but less rushed**, able to check training carefully and keep ordinary plans under review.
S3.quote: Five years lets me learn something properly instead of buying the first course with an impressive title.
fieldNote: His **longer warning** changes the pace of preparation, without making possible income loss disappear from the mood assessment.
The **association proposal** seeks named paid tasks behind training, while household reviews remain quarterly rather than an immediate cancellation of plans.

steps.text: Take the checked servicing course using the separate learning pot
Save an extra hundred monthly when bills permit
Attend two association meetings to draft paid-training proposals
Trial fault-planning software on paid crew time after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us no excuse to leave training until somebody's final payslip. I'd support a public training fund with employers putting money in too. I'd write to our local representative rather than assume a trade meeting alone can pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My income looks secure over the next few years because most of my day is still physical repair. By 2036 the planning work changes, then robots follow around 2039, when I'll be forty. I feel better with that runway, though I can't promise myself that maintenance will always escape automation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the same checked course now, but give myself a year to practise alongside repair work instead of chasing a new title immediately. I'd write next month asking for a jointly funded paid-training scheme. In the first year after 2036 I'd use the planning tools on paid jobs, then review actual robot prices and service demand before spending anything on machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy rather than scared about my wages now. I can imagine an ordinary next few years, with a reason to keep learning instead of a deadline pressing against my chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not buy a small robot as soon as one is offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A machine without paying work is an expensive ornament. I'd want to see service contracts, repairs, insurance and the real purchase price; I don't have those numbers today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in the letter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd describe how an unpaid week makes training impossible for someone with no savings, even when the course itself is free. Our four-month cushion helps us, but I work beside people who can't miss a day's pay.

say: I'd support a **public training fund** with employers contributing money too.
I'd write to a **local representative** rather than assume trade meetings can fund paid learning.
think: My **near-term income** looks secure because physical repairs still occupy most of my day.
I have longer to prepare for **2036 planning changes** and robots around 2039, without assuming maintenance stays safe forever.
do: Take the **checked servicing course** and practise alongside repairs for a year.
Write next month requesting **jointly funded training** that keeps people paid.
Use **planning tools** on paid jobs after 2036 before reviewing actual robot costs and demand.
feel: **Uneasy but unhurried**, expecting ordinary working years while preparing for later changes.
S4.quote: A machine without paying work is an expensive ornament.
fieldNote: He feels **near-term security** with a decade's warning, but will still be working age when capable physical robots arrive.
His **policy request** names paid time as well as course costs, while any machine purchase waits for evidence he lacks today.

steps.text: Take the checked servicing course and practise alongside paid repairs
Write next month requesting a jointly funded paid-training scheme
Use new planning tools on paid repair jobs after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the planning changes could squeeze our prices before training catches up. Paid practical learning linked to actual work would help, with the crew and office staff involved in choosing it. I'd want a short-term income bridge if the paid visits disappear while I train.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets the spare hour when a job becomes quicker. I like new tools, but I don't want my apprentice learning twice as fast only to spend twice as long unemployed. Better tools should leave room to teach someone properly.

headlineQuote: Ask who gets the spare hour when a job becomes quicker.
portrait: Rafael is a **27-year-old crew lead** with a technical diploma and master licence, wiring homes and repairing shops.
He rents with **partner Jules**, has four months saved, earns typical pay and can reach a few other contractors.
He uses **AI daily** and wants saved time shared through practical training and a voice for office staff.
The quick AGI picture makes him **anxious about income**, while longer warnings allow checked courses, saving and association work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could squeeze repair prices before workers have time to complete useful training.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid practical learning** linked to actual work should include both crew members and office staff.
A **short-term income bridge** would help if paid visits disappear while he trains.
